nodes.s: The dot in the middle is where the player is right now. Not a rank. Not a level. A state.
nodes.m: Everything on this map points at this dot. Four functions act on it from around the circle. The fifth, Pathway, reaches it only when an institution puts something at risk. The question you use to read the map is fit: does what this player needs right now match what this place actually does? The dot moves. It is supposed to.

nodes.s: Soccer for its own sake. Pickup, rec league, the backyard. No one is measuring. This is where love of the game is made, and the one function that never closes.
nodes.m: Six-year-olds live here. Forty-year-olds live here. Pros come back here on their day off. Recreation is cheap, local, and answers the only question that matters at the start: do you want to play again tomorrow? What happens here: touches, friends, freedom, a scoreboard nobody writes down. The risk: adults turning it into a test too early. Where it goes: into Test when the player wants more, into the Adult Game for life, and back here from everywhere else on the map.

nodes.s: Games that count. Standings, scores, a bracket. Competition tells you how you stack up today. That is all it tells you.
nodes.m: Competition answers one question: how do you do against others, under pressure, right now? It does not develop you by itself. It reveals. Travel leagues, tournaments and showcases are all competition. They cost the most and get the most attention because they are visible. What happens here: wins, losses, nerves, playing time decisions, the first time a result makes someone cry in a car. The risk: paying for competition and believing you bought development.

nodes.s: Where the player actually gets better. Training, repetition, feedback, time. Slow, unglamorous, and the only function that compounds.
nodes.m: Development is deliberate work on the player: technique, decisions, body, mind. It can happen at a club, with a trainer, on a phone screen, in a garage with a wall. It is the function families most want and most often fail to get, because it hides inside programs sold as competition. What happens here: thousands of repetitions, corrections, plateaus, a breakthrough, another plateau. The risk: mistaking being busy (practices, games, travel) for getting better.

nodes.s: Someone picks. Tryouts, cuts, rosters, ID camps, recruiting. Selection sorts players into rooms. It says nothing about who they will become.
nodes.m: Selection is a sorting event run by someone else with their own needs: a roster to fill, a position to cover, a budget to hit. It happens at 8, at 12, at 16, at 18, at 22, and again every year of a working life. It is the function with the most emotion and the least information. What happens here: a yes or a no, often with no explanation. The risk: treating a selection decision as a judgment of worth instead of a fit decision made by a stranger with a spreadsheet.

nodes.s: The moment play starts to count. Usually age 8 to 10. The first handoff, and the one most families rush.
nodes.m: What breaks here: a child who loved playing meets a scoreboard, a coach who wants to win, and parents on a sideline. Some thrive. Many go quiet. The question to ask: does this child want this test, or do we? Stay signals: still begging to play after games. Move signals: asking for more, not less. Step back signals: stomach aches before games, silence in the car.

nodes.s: When competing stops being enough and the player needs to actually improve. The handoff most programs skip.
nodes.m: What breaks here: families keep buying more competition (another league, another tournament) when the player needs repetition and feedback. The question: what is my child working on, and who is working on it with them? If nobody can answer, you are standing at this gate and haven't crossed it. Crossing it is often cheap: a wall, a ball, a plan, a person who corrects you.

nodes.s: Taking developed ability into a room where someone picks. Where the stakes get loud.
nodes.m: What breaks here: a player who has been developing well gets evaluated in forty minutes by someone who needs a left back. The question: what does this room need, and is that what we are? Prepare for the test as a test. Don't let the outcome rewrite the development that got you here.

nodes.s: After a selection, picked or not, the player goes back to playing. This gate is always open. Most people forget it exists.
nodes.m: What happens here: the player returns to the ball without a scoreboard. For a picked player, this keeps love of the game alive under pressure. For an unpicked one, this is where the real decision gets made: do I still want to play? If yes, the map is still open. If no, the map is still open, just with different roads. This gate also leads straight into the Adult Game, at any age.

nodes.s: Pathway isn't a stage you climb to. It's a condition. It switches on when an institution risks something on the player: money, a roster spot, a reputation. Then, usually, it switches off.
nodes.m: An academy that waives fees. A college that pays for school. A club that signs a contract. Each one is bearing risk, and that is what makes it pathway. It can begin at 12 or at 22 or never. It ends the moment the risk is withdrawn, which is most of the time, for most players. You don't carry pathway. It carries you, for a while. Five functions shape the player. Four sit around the dot. Pathway arrives when an institution risks something on them.

nodes.s: The no. At 12, 16, 18, or 22. The most common event on this map and the one nobody prepares for.
nodes.m: What it is: a fit decision by a stranger with needs. What it isn't: a measure of who you are or will be. Almost everyone who does anything in the game was told no at least once, usually more. The roads from here go everywhere: back into the field at Play or Learn, into College Country, into the Adult Game, into the Working Game, straight into Beyond. Pick one. Then pick another later if you want.

nodes.s: The body says no. Sometimes for a season, sometimes for good.
nodes.m: What happens: rehab, watching, an identity that shakes. Rehab is development, just aimed at the body, so the player is still in Learn. Injured players make sharp analysts and coaches because they spend a season watching. Roads: back into Learn, into the Working Game through performance and medical, or into Beyond with body literacy most people never get.

nodes.s: The family can't pay for the next level. Common. Rarely said out loud.
nodes.m: In a pay-to-play system money is a function of its own, sitting under all the others. What happens: the family quietly drops down or out, and tells the child it's about something else. Roads: Recreation never closes and never costs much. Low-cost development (pickup, a wall, video, a plan) is real development. Scholarships inside College Country are the Pathway route. Say it plainly in the family and plan from there.

nodes.s: The right program is three hours away. Or in another country.
nodes.m: Distance decides more careers than talent does. What happens: a family does the math on hours, gas and siblings, and the answer is usually no. Roads: stay local and develop (Learn is portable, Choose is not), or move, which is a family decision and not a soccer one. Either road is legitimate. Only one gets talked about.

nodes.s: The player stops wanting it. Usually after years of adults wanting it for them.
nodes.m: Wanting to stop is information, not failure. What happens: the player goes quiet, gets injured more, finds reasons to miss. Roads: The Way Back gate (play with no scoreboard, no adults watching), a real break with a door left open, the Adult Game later when it's theirs again. Many players who stop at 15 are back at 25 and play until they're 60.

nodes.s: A club covers the cost and gives a spot. Training most days, school arranged around it. The club is betting on you. Bets get called.
nodes.m: This is pathway at 12 to 18. What happens: full-time training, travel, a schedule run by the club, and an annual decision about whether the bet continues. Most academy players are released before a pro contract. The good ones leave with development nobody can take back and a clear road into College Country.

nodes.s: A college pays for some or all of school because of soccer. Backed, but renewed year to year. This is pathway inside College Country.
nodes.m: What happens: a roster spot and money with conditions attached: grades, fitness, the coach staying, the program keeping its budget. Partial scholarships are the norm. The real product is still the degree. The soccer is the way it gets paid for.

nodes.s: A club pays you to play. First contracts are usually short and small. The real product is the next contract.
nodes.m: What happens: training is the job, performance is reviewed constantly, and the contract has an end date on the front page. Most first contracts are not renewed. The road out of here is the most important one on the map, and the one players prepare for least. Playing careers end for everyone. Usually sooner than planned.

nodes.s: The club says no. The risk is withdrawn. This happens to most backed players at some point.
nodes.m: Not a verdict. A budget decision, a coaching change, a glut at your position, an injury at the wrong time. Roads: another club (trials), College Country if age allows, the Adult Game, the Working Game where your inside knowledge is worth money, or Beyond with a stack of attributes most people never earn.

nodes.s: A two-week audition at a club somewhere else. Lower divisions across Europe, Scandinavia, Asia, Australia take players who are good and mobile.
nodes.m: What happens: culture, language, money up front, no guarantee. You will be judged against locals the coach already knows. What you take: range, independence, and a map in your head of how the sport works everywhere. Some of the best careers in the Working Game started as failed trials.

nodes.s: College coaches pick from showcases, video, emails and relationships. A selection function with a long timeline and its own language.
nodes.m: Starts at 15 or 16 for the most visible players, later for everyone else. What happens: emails sent, camps paid for, coaches who watch and don't call. The question: what does this program need next year, not what do they say they value? Roads: the scholarship, the walk-on, the club team, or a different school entirely.

nodes.s: D1, D2, D3, NAIA, JUCO. Not a ranking of quality. A set of rules about money, time and seasons.
nodes.m: D1 and D2 can offer athletic money. D3 cannot but often offers academic money that adds up to more. NAIA has its own rules. JUCO is two years, cheaper, and a real road into any of the others. Players move between all of them. Fit beats prestige every time, and the player who picks on fit usually plays more.

nodes.s: You make the roster without being recruited. Nobody held a spot for you. You earn one from inside.
nodes.m: What happens: you prove it in preseason against players the coach already chose. Some walk-ons end up backed. Most don't and play anyway. What you take: how to enter a room nobody held for you, which is most rooms in a working life.

nodes.s: College soccer without the varsity label. Competition, travel, friends. Not a consolation. The adult game starting early.
nodes.m: Most college students who play, play here. Club teams travel, compete in national brackets and are run by the players themselves, which is leadership and operations training nobody calls that. Roads: straight into the Adult Game, and into the Working Game through the organizing you did without noticing.

nodes.s: Changing schools to change fit. Common now. A second selection event, this time with real information about what you need.
nodes.m: What happens: a year of knowing what didn't work, then a new recruiting process run by a player who finally knows what to ask. Transfers up and down are both normal. The question is the same as everywhere: what do I need now, and does this place do that?

nodes.s: The actual product of College Country. The game got you in the door. The degree is what walks out.
nodes.m: What you take into Beyond: proof you can finish something hard over four years while being evaluated constantly, and a calendar discipline most graduates never built. Roads from here: a pro draft or trial (rare), the Adult Game (most), the Working Game (many), Beyond (everyone, eventually).

nodes.s: A few players leave college into pro contracts. Most don't. Plan for both, in that order of likelihood.
nodes.m: What happens: a draft or a trial, a short contract or a no. Even the yes is usually a small contract with a short end date. The degree is why the no is survivable. Roads: Pro Contract, semi-pro while you try again, or the rest of the map.

nodes.s: Show up, play, go home. The purest Play on the map. Every city has it and it costs nothing.
nodes.m: What happens: strangers become teammates, nobody keeps the score for long, and the best player on the field is often fifty. Someone has to organize it, though, which is leadership with no title and no pay. Pickup is where many adults rediscover why they ever played.

nodes.s: Organized, cheap, competitive enough. Teams last decades. This is where the game lives for most adults who still play.
nodes.m: What happens: a season, a table, a kit, a group chat. Play and Test, a little Learn, almost no Choose. Roads: futsal, over-30s, coaching your kid, running the league, which is the Working Game by accident.

nodes.s: Indoor, fast, more touches per minute than anything else on the map. Development disguised as fun.
nodes.m: What happens: the ball comes back every three seconds and the decisions never stop. Players of every age get sharper here without anybody calling it training. It's also one of the cheapest doors on the map for a kid whose family can't afford the travel team.

nodes.kind: Serious soccer for people with jobs
nodes.s: Regional leagues where you might get gas money. Serious soccer for people with day jobs. A real road back toward Pathway for a few.
nodes.m: What happens: training two nights a week, games on weekends, a job on Monday. Some players get spotted here and signed. Most play because it's the highest level that still fits a life. Both are legitimate.

nodes.kind: The game adapts to the body
nodes.s: The game changes shape to fit the body. Over-30s, over-40s, over-50s, walking football. You can play into your 70s.
nodes.m: What happens: different rules, slower speeds, the same feeling. The people here have been on every other plate on this map and came back. That's the strongest argument for Recreation there is.

nodes.s: You come back into Play as the adult on the sideline. Everything on this map now applies to someone you love.
nodes.m: What happens: you volunteer for a U8 team, and every handoff you ever went through comes back with the stakes reversed. This is the most common way adults re-enter the field and the most common entry into the Working Game. Roads: back to Play, or the coaching ladder.

nodes.s: Volunteer to licensed to paid. Selection happens here too: someone hires you.
nodes.m: Its own five functions: coach a U8 team this Saturday (play), your team's results get judged (test), licenses, mentors, hours (learn), a club hires you (choose), and pathway begins when a club pays you full time and bets its program on you. Former players start with credibility. Non-players start with patience. Both get hired.

nodes.kind: The clearest ladder on the map
nodes.s: Grassroots to pro. The one road with a clear ladder, a shortage of people, and pay at every rung.
nodes.m: What happens: a course, a badge, a Saturday of U10 games, and a path that is assessed and promoted on a schedule. The skill is reading the game and communicating under pressure while everyone disagrees with you. Teenagers can start. Adults can start.

nodes.kind: Reading the game as a job
nodes.s: Video, numbers, scouting reports. Reading the game is the skill. The game already taught you that.
nodes.m: What happens: hours of footage, patterns nobody else saw, a report a coach actually uses. Entry is cheap: free footage, free tools, a public account. Pathway begins when a club pays for the reports.

nodes.s: Watching players and making the fit call. You now run the selection function you once feared.
nodes.m: What happens: cold fields, long drives, a judgment about a fourteen-year-old that will change their map. People who were told no are often the best at this, because they know what the no does and what it doesn't mean.

nodes.s: Camera, mic, keyboard. Low cost of entry, high competition. Telling the game's stories to people who care.
nodes.m: What happens: you publish, the market scores you in views and trust, you get better by doing it a thousand times. Pathway begins when someone pays you to do it. Players who can explain the game have an edge nobody can buy.

nodes.s: Registrations, fields, schedules, sponsors, budgets. The machinery under the map, where most of the money decisions get made.
nodes.m: What happens: a club is a small business with a season for a fiscal year. The director of operations decides more about which kids get to play than any coach does. Former Sunday league treasurers walk into this job all the time.

nodes.s: Standing between players and clubs. You need to read the whole map to do this well.
nodes.m: What happens: contracts, trials, phone calls at midnight, a player's family trusting you with their map. The good ones know every plate here, especially the Crossroads, because that's where most clients end up.

nodes.s: Athletic training, physio, strength, nutrition. You've been the patient. Now you're the practitioner.
nodes.m: What happens: school, licenses, a training room, a body in front of you that you understand from the inside. This is the Working Game's door into medicine proper, and a lot of people walk through it.

nodes.kind: The people who draw the map
nodes.s: Rules, competitions, governance. The people who decide what the map looks like for everyone else.
nodes.m: What happens: meetings, policy, budgets, a thousand small rules that decide where the handoffs sit and how much they cost. If you think the system should work differently, this is the plate where that gets decided.

nodes.s: Owning a piece of a club or a company in the game. You become the institution that makes pathway exist for someone else.
nodes.m: What happens: capital at risk, a board, a budget, and the decision about which players the club bets on. The gold road on this map exists because someone here chose to bear risk. That's the whole loop.

nodes.s: Every industry has people doing it for love with no scoreboard. Garage bands, home cooks, weekend coders, kids reading anatomy for fun. That's Recreation.
nodes.m: The size and health of an industry's hobbyist function predicts a lot about it. Industries that make hobbyists feel welcome have deep benches. Industries that gatekeep them run out of people.

nodes.s: Where the work gets scored by someone else. Sales numbers, reviews, court rulings, pitch meetings, board exams. That's Competition.
nodes.m: Markets reveal, they don't develop. An industry that confuses the two burns through people the way a youth club that only plays tournaments does.

nodes.s: School, apprenticeships, licenses, reps. The function that compounds, in every field.
nodes.m: Ask of any industry: where do people actually get better, and who pays for it? The answer tells you who gets to rise.

nodes.s: Interviews, admissions, auditions, funding rounds. Strangers with needs sorting people into rooms. That's Selection.
nodes.m: Same rules as a tryout. The room has a need. Fit, not worth. A no is information. Players who learned this at 14 walk into their first job interview with a ten-year head start.

nodes.s: An employer pays you. An investor funds you. A firm makes you partner. Someone bears risk on you. That is pathway in any industry.
nodes.m: Until then you are on the field, and the field is where almost everyone is almost all the time. Knowing the difference between being developed and being backed is the most useful thing this map teaches.

evidence.line: About 6 of 100 high school boys and 8 of 100 girls go on to play NCAA soccer (DI 1.4 / 2.8, DII 1.7 / 2.2, DIII 2.8 / 3.0).
evidence.note: Comparison of two annual counts, not a cohort. Club-only players are not in the 100, so the true rate is lower.

evidence.line: About 3 of 100 high school boys and 5 of 100 girls reach NCAA Division I or II, the divisions that can offer athletic money.
evidence.note: Reaching DI or DII is not the same as a full scholarship. Since the House settlement, soccer rosters are capped at 28 with no sport-specific scholarship caps.

evidence.pop: youth athletes after ACL reconstruction (mean age 14)
evidence.line: After an ACL reconstruction, 79 of 100 young athletes return to their previous level and 92 of 100 return to some sport. Up to 32 of 100 suffer a second ACL injury.
evidence.note: One injury type only. Adults return to prior level at 65 of 100. No comparable data for concussion, growth-plate or overuse injuries.

evidence.line: About 1 of 100 NCAA men's seniors is taken in the MLS SuperDraft (90 picks in December 2025). On the women's side there is no draft since 2024; roughly 30 to 45 college players sign NWSL deals a year, under 1 of 100 seniors.
evidence.note: Picks are published; the eligible pool (about 6,500 to 7,500 men) is estimated from NCAA participation. Women's figure is modeled from reported signings.

evidence.line: 12 of 100 SuperDraft picks (11 of 90) had signed an MLS first-team contract by March 2026.
evidence.note: Partial-season tally; signings continue through the year.

evidence.line: 39 of 100 SuperDraft picks signed in the second or third tier instead: 32 of 90 with MLS NEXT Pro or USL League One, 3 with USL Championship.
evidence.note: Most drafted players start below the first team.

evidence.pop: players in the 30 MLS academies (U15 to U19)
evidence.line: Somewhere between 5 and 15 of 100 MLS academy players get professional minutes with MLS NEXT Pro. 1,300+ academy players have appeared since 2022, and 200 MLS NEXT Pro players have signed MLS first-team deals in four seasons.
evidence.note: Numerators are published; the academy pool (roughly 1,000 to 1,500 listed players at a time) is modeled from the 35-per-club limit. The other 243 Elite Academies are not in this 100.

evidence.line: Fewer than 1 of 100 MLS NEXT players sign an MLS Homegrown contract: 30 Homegrown debuts in 2026 so far against 43,000+ players, and 483 since 2008.
evidence.note: Most MLS NEXT players are not in an MLS academy; the rate for the 30 MLS academies is far higher (see Academy Place to Pro Contract).

evidence.line: About 1 to 2 of 100 registered youth players are in MLS NEXT (43,000+ players against 2.68 million US Youth Soccer registrations). The girls' side is unknown: ECNL and Girls Academy publish club counts, not players.
evidence.note: Registrations overlap across bodies, so the 100 is approximate.

evidence.pop: children who played soccer in the year
evidence.line: Roughly 40 to 65 of 100 children who play soccer are registered with a sanctioning body. US Youth Soccer alone registers 2.68 million; U.S. Soccer's audit shows $6.6 million in membership and registration fees at $1 per registered youth or adult player, so all member bodies together register no more than about 6 million people, against roughly 7 million kids 6 to 17 who played.
evidence.note: Registrations overlap across bodies and include adults and recreational programs, so the share in competitive club play is lower. The $1-per-player fee is stated in the audit's notes; the revenue line also includes organizational and pro-league fees.

evidence.pop: registered youth players in three state associations (NC, GA, IN)
evidence.line: About 38 of 100 registered youth players are on a team they had to be picked for. Coding three state registrars' own categories onto the functions: recreation is PLAY, every tryout-selected tier (classic, challenge, travel, select) is TEST. North Carolina 41 of 100, Indiana 39, Georgia 30, weighted 38 across 155,883 players.
evidence.note: The first function-coded number on the Field. Registration category is a proxy for function: a travel roster can still be a developmental environment. SFIA's CORE share (38 of 100 play 26+ days a year) corroborates it from a different direction. In North Carolina, 205 players moved from recreation onto a competitive or academy roster mid-season, 0.7 of 100 recreation players; most moves happen at tryouts, which registrars do not log.

alt.label: in a tryout-selected tier in North Carolina alone

evidence.line: U.S. Soccer's own figure: around 70 of 100 children who play soccer have quit by age 14, and almost half of 9 to 11 year olds say they are likely to quit within the next year.
evidence.note: Cumulative attrition from early entry, not a one-season rate. The 9 to 11 figure is stated intent, not observed exit. The federation publishes no breakdown of where they go.

alt.label: of 9 to 11 year olds likely to quit within a year

evidence.period: McKinsey and U.S. Soccer research, reported 2025
evidence.trend: 3x: Latino and Black children vs white children, stopping because they felt unwelcome
evidence.line: Research by McKinsey and U.S. Soccer found Latino and Black children are three times more likely than white children to stop playing soccer because they feel unwelcome. Burnout is not only tiredness; sometimes it is the room.
evidence.note: A relative risk, not a rate. Reported through the Aspen Institute and NBC; the underlying McKinsey work is not public in full. This is why the season check-in now has "didn't feel welcome" as a reason for leaving.

evidence.line: About 2 of 100 adults who play soccer are registered in an adult league (229,698 USASA registrations against roughly 11 million adult outdoor players). Almost all adult soccer is pickup and unregistered.
evidence.note: Adult share of the 16.8 million outdoor players is estimated from SFIA age bands.

evidence.pop: adult outdoor soccer players by age
evidence.line: Adults are coming back. Outdoor soccer play among 35 to 44 year olds grew 118% from 2018 to 2025, and 247% among 45 to 54 year olds.
evidence.note: Growth, not a rate. SFIA reads this as re-entry by the first youth-soccer generation.

evidence.line: 21 of 100 six-year-olds play soccer, more than any other sport, and the share falls every year after. Across ages 6 to 17, 14 of 100 played in the past year.
evidence.note: Entry is the one road soccer wins. Retention is the problem.

alt.label: ages 6 to 17 who played soccer in the past year

facts.h: Does anyone track players moving between the five functions?
facts.body: No. No public source follows a player from one function to the next. Registrars count who is in each program once a year; they do not count who crossed. Nobody registers training, so TEST to LEARN is invisible. Tryouts are run by thousands of clubs and nobody aggregates who showed up or who was cut, so LEARN to CHOOSE is invisible. Only the last leg, CHOOSE to PATHWAY, has numbers, because institutions publish rosters, and even those give the destination, never the origin. Every data holder counts the people inside its own walls; movement happens between walls, and no one owns that space. This site measures it two ways: coding registrations by function (the stocks) and the season check-in (the flows).

facts.h: How many people play soccer in the U.S.?
facts.body: 16.8 million Americans aged 6 and over played outdoor soccer in 2025, a record, up 15.8% in a year. 6.6 million played indoor. 5.5 million of the outdoor players were children aged 6 to 12.

facts.h: How many play high school soccer?
facts.body: 877,956 in 2024-25: 484,908 boys at 12,969 schools and 393,048 girls at 12,516 schools.
28,746 men and 31,200 women in 2024-25. Division III has the most programs (406 men's, 416 women's). NAIA adds about 190 men's and 197 women's programs; 48 of 100 NAIA men are international.
273 clubs, 2,189 teams and 43,000+ players in 2025-26; 318 clubs and 53,000+ players in 2026-27. 30 of those clubs are MLS academies.

$910 a year on average per child (Aspen, 2025). 26.9 of 100 participants say out-of-pocket cost has changed how they take part. The gap in regular play between the highest and lowest income tiers widened to 24.8 points in 2025.

facts.h: At what age does each function usually start?
facts.body: Recreation: almost everyone enters here, usually at 4 to 7 (U6 is the youngest standard age group). Competition: tryout-based travel teams usually start at 8 to 10, with 9v9 at U11 and U12. Development: training as its own program usually begins at 12 to 13; MLS NEXT's youngest age group is U13, and clubs run pre-academy programs below that. Selection: tryouts happen every year from the first travel team, but the high-stakes window is 13 to 16: MLS NEXT runs talent ID at U13 and U14, and NCAA Division I coaches may first contact a player on June 15 after sophomore year. Pathway: academy backing from about 13, college from 18. Two skips exist and are rare: competition straight to selection, and development straight to pathway. Ages are program rules and common practice, not a measured cohort.

facts.h: Of 100 registered youth players, how many sit in each function?
facts.body: Coding three state associations' registration categories onto the functions (155,883 players, NC, GA and IN): PLAY 57 (recreation and TOPSoccer), TEST 38 (every tier you must be picked for: classic, challenge, travel, select), LEARN 5 (North Carolina's developmental academy tier; the other two states do not separate it). CHOOSE is an event, not a place to be registered, so it shows up as the 38 who passed through a tryout. PATHWAY is not in state registration at all. Private trainers, camps and futsal are invisible to registrars, so LEARN is undercounted.

facts.h: How many players change clubs during a season?
facts.body: North Carolina's registrar logs it. In the 2024-25 season, 529 competitive and academy players (1.6 of 100) were released by their association mid-season and 336 (1.0 of 100) re-rostered with a new one; 570 moved between teams inside their club; 961 were dual-rostered and 3,079 used a club pass to play up or across teams (5 of 100 of all registered players). This is the only published, player-level movement log found so far at any state association, and it covers a single state's in-season moves, not the tryout window where most movement happens.

facts.h: What does the whole youth system cost, and who could pay?
facts.body: Families spend about $1,188 a year on soccer (Aspen, 2022 data) and roughly 4 million youth players are registered, so the system runs on something like $4 to 5 billion of family money a year. U.S. Soccer's entire budget was $264 million of revenue and $262 million of expenses in fiscal 2025, about 5 cents on every dollar families spend. Nobody is in a position to make the whole thing free.

Soccer draws 21 of 100 six-year-olds, then loses share every year after. U.S. Soccer's own figure is that around 70 of 100 have quit by age 14, and almost half of 9 to 11 year olds say they are likely to quit within a year. Nobody counts the reason at the moment it happens; that is what the season check-in on this site measures.
About 126,000 U.S. Soccer referee licenses in 2024, almost all grassroots. Secondhand figure from a State Referee Committee workshop slide; no source links referees to a playing history.

facts.h: How many adults play in registered leagues?
facts.body: 229,698 USASA registrations in 2024, plus 22,003 through USSSA. Against about 11 million adult outdoor players, registered league play is about 2 of 100.
